extracted.intended_audience: CRTC Commissioners, CRTC staff, communications regulators, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and recommended procedural standards for how an administrative communications tribunal (CRTC) should make, draft, review, publish and revise decisions in broadcasting and telecommunications matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioners should write decisions they hear
rubrics_metrics.description: Accordingly, it would seem highly desirable for the Commissioners hearing applications to not only decide them but, where possible, to write the decisions as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing decisions would force Commissioners to consider all facts and arguments carefully, ensure relevant factors are weighed, and increase personal responsibility for decisions. The report proposes panels meet immediately after hearings to prepare rough outlines with reasons; staff assist with data; a full-time member prepares complete drafts, circulates them for revisions, and decisions are released within four to six weeks. The drafting member should not be assigned further hearings until this work is completed. Secretariat continues to prepare routine/non-appearing items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid staff acting as decision-makers
rubrics_metrics.description: To the extent staff members do this, they become decision-makers, a function which should, of course, be exclusively that of the Commissioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When staff are required to 'flesh out' reasons because Commissioners have not fully spelled them out, staff may inappropriately assume decision-making roles. Procedures should minimize staff initiative in finding supporting rationale and keep the primary decision-making responsibility with Commissioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-hearing drafting process and timeframes
rubrics_metrics.description: At the conclusion of the hearing, the panel would meet and review the applications they had heard. Sufficient time would be set aside ... to permit the Commissioners to prepare rough outlines of decisions ... Having completed outlines of decisions, the panel members would then disperse. The full-time members would return to Ottawa and one of them would have the responsibility of preparing complete drafts ... The decisions would then be released and the process would be completed within four to six weeks following the hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed recommended steps: panel meeting immediately after hearing to draft outlines (1–2 days), staff assistance to gather data, full-time member prepares full draft and circulates to other members, telephone or meeting consultations to settle revisions, release within 4–6 weeks. The drafting member shouldn't be assigned other hearings until finished. Secretariat handles routine items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of expression, terminology and policy positions
rubrics_metrics.description: There might be concerns ... about achieving consistency of expression and policy positions where nine Commissioners theoretically would be writing decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concern can be addressed by assigning staff decision-writing team members and senior staff to Commissioners during the initial period to ensure consistency of style, terminology and arguments. However, while consistency is desirable, it is not essential provided meaning is clear and 'terms of art' are given a uniform meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism for internal Executive Committee review
rubrics_metrics.description: A mechanism for review of decisions by the Executive Committee either on its own motion or that of a party to an application would permit decisions to be changed which the Executive Committee as a whole considered to have been wrongly taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a mechanism would allow the Executive Committee to change decisions based on specified criteria (see criteria rubrics). It also would serve as a check on hearing panels if those panels are granted greater autonomy. The power should be used sparingly and according to established criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for exercising review: error in law or fact
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission announced that it would exercise its powers under section 63 where an applicant demonstrated on a prima facie basis one or more of the following: an error in law or fact ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An applicant seeking review must demonstrate, prima facie, an error in law or fact in the original decision. This is one of the explicit grounds that justify review, rescission, or variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for exercising review: fundamental change in circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission announced that it would exercise its powers ... where an applicant demonstrated ... a fundamental change in circumstances or facts since the decision ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If circumstances or facts fundamental to the original decision have materially changed since that decision, that change can justify reopening or varying the decision under the review power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for exercising review: failure to consider a basic principle raised
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission announced that it would exercise its powers ... where an applicant demonstrated ... a failure to consider a basic principle that had been raised in the original proceeding ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the original proceeding failed to consider a basic principle that had in fact been raised, that omission may support review of the decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for exercising review: emergence of a new principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission announced that it would exercise its powers ... where an applicant demonstrated ... that a new principle had arisen as a result of the decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the decision itself gives rise to a new legal or policy principle not previously contemplated, that can justify reappraisal under the review mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for exercising review: substantial doubt as to correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: It was noted that section 63 would also permit the Commission to determine that there was substantial doubt as to the correctness of its original decision and that reappraisal was accordingly warranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where substantial doubt exists about the correctness of the original decision (even absent the other enumerated grounds), the Commission may reappraise and vary or rescind the decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limit on exercise of review power
rubrics_metrics.description: However, a time limit, which is now absent in section 63, should be imposed on the exercise of this power ... A period of 60 days, for example, would coincide with the time now permitted to the Governor-in-Council ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend imposing a finite period (example: 60 days) within which the Executive Committee (or equivalent) may exercise review/rescission powers to avoid ongoing uncertainty for licensees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation of final decision-making authority to hearing panels
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be necessary to amend section 19 of the Broadcasting Act to provide public hearing panels with the power to make decisions on behalf of the Commission ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposal: statutorily or administratively empower hearing panels to make final decisions (and write them). To address consultation requirements, remove or amend provisions requiring consultation with part-time members (section 17). Alternatively, use administrative procedures to table and briefly discuss panel decisions at full Commission meetings to satisfy consultation, then have Executive Committee review/adopt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative procedure alternative to statutory amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: These changes could also be substantially implemented without statutory amendments by adopting administrative procedures that would accomplish the same ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example administrative flow: panel makes and writes decision; table at full Commission to satisfy consultation with part-time members; table at next Executive Committee meeting for review and adoption; decisions released immediately after Executive Committee adopts them; panel decisions to carry decisive weight and be varied only in exceptional circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishing dissenting opinions in appropriate cases
rubrics_metrics.description: It would seem desirable, therefore for the CRTC in appropriate cases to continue to publish the dissenting opinions of the Commissioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments for publication: allows full exposition of differing policy views, helps define issues clearly, assists licensees and the public to understand policy thinking. Arguments against: may undermine a unified public position, require staff resources. The report recommends allowing publication in appropriate cases and notes the proposed scheme would facilitate their writing since Commissioners prepare reasons themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow oral decisions for simple or uncontested matters
rubrics_metrics.description: In broadcasting applications, there are many instances where the applications involve simple or uncontested issues and it would be entirely appropriate for the hearing panel to give a decision from the bench.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oral decisions could be given from the bench for simple/uncontested items; panel may call a short recess to consult and agree on reasons, or allocate time at end of day to decide items and announce decisions the following morning. In telecommunications, oral decisions may be possible for narrow tariff items. Benefits: expedites process, parties know decisions immediately, frees Commissioners for complex cases. Statutory changes may be required to vest panels with final decision power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish written procedures for petitions to Cabinet with notice/opportunity to respond
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no written procedures for presenting petitions to Cabinet but certain practices have been established ... The procedures that have been established do not require that any of the parties to the proceeding from which the matter arises be given notice of the petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current informal practices permit petitions by letter/brief and Department prepares a memorandum, often without notice to other parties. The report criticizes lack of notice/opportunity to respond and suggests that written procedures should be adopted so parties can be informed and may file comments. Department typically solicits CRTC comments, but other interested party comments may or may not be taken into account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure transparency and fairness when higher-level political review occurs
rubrics_metrics.description: From the point of view of the procedures which the CRTC employs in its hearings, this process can play havoc with principles of fairness ... This hearing process ... appears to be a futile exercise if a body which has not participated in the process ... can vary or set aside the decision, perhaps on the basis of grounds that were not raised during the hearing and to which none of the parties were given an opportunity to speak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political review (e.g., Cabinet petitions) should not peremptorily reverse fully litigated, open decisions without providing parties notice and an opportunity to be heard. Reversal in secret partisan processes undermines fairness; any political appeal should be exercised openly and with opportunity for affected parties to comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit political second-guessing to preserve tribunal independence and decision quality
rubrics_metrics.description: My opposition is based on four inter-related grounds: First ... Second ... Third ... Fourth ... (political appeals undermine rationale for administrative tribunals; are hit-and-miss; diminish quality of decisions and persons willing to serve; are incompatible with judicial processes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political interventions should be rare and constrained because they: undermine the rationale for specialized adjudication; are subject to political vagaries; can lower decision quality and deter qualified members; and blend incompatible political and judicial processes. The report recommends limiting such interventions and confining review to narrow, well-defined criteria and time limits.
